To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ammonium (a major component of acid deposition) concentrations in air and in precipitation at the Institute in New York declined over a period of 14 years (1984-2000), but increased in 2001.

NH4+ and SO42- in precipitation and air were correlated over an 18 year period in New York State and at 31 other sites in the Eastern United States and that NH4+ in precipitation increased in New York State in the last 3 years of the study, while SO42- decreased.

NH(4)(4) concentrations in air and in precipitation at the IES site in southeastern New York declined over an 8 year period from 1984 to 1999 but increased from 1989 to 2000, and that the NH(4)(-) trends correlated well with SO(2)(-) trends over the 8 year period, but were not well correlated with local agricultural NH(3) emission.

the effects of acid deposition on forest ecosystems and the role of atmospheric nitrogen (N) in the acidification of forest soils and streams.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
reductions in S deposition have reduced the NH(4)(+)/NH(4)(+)N deposition in the northeastern U. S.

reductions in S deposition have reduced N deposition, which has led to a decrease in N availability and thus a reduction in N leaching from the soil and a reduction in N emissions from soils to the atmosphere.

the reduction in SO2 emissions has reduced NH4+ transport to the Northeast.
